prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B017 alone, credited to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The scientific case is a continuous chain from human incretin physiology (Holst), through proglucagon processing and receptor biology (Drucker), to the bioactive GLP-1(7-36) peptide (Mojsov), and on to therapies with randomized outcome evidence in glycaemia, body weight, cardiovascular and renal endpoints. It is original, independently confirmed over decades and mature. The round-1 exchange sharpened one point for me: the citation should state the principle that the prize rewards the discovery of the hormone's physiology and its active form, and that the long-acting analogues followed from that discovery. Worded this way the omission of Knudsen is a stated boundary of the award, not an oversight, and the citation does not claim to cover drug design.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weak point and I do not think the round-1 exchange resolved it. Priority for the active peptide and its insulinotropic role (Mojsov versus Habener and others) is not settled by the supplied evidence, so Mojsov is the least secure of the three names. Knudsen's acylation design produced the drugs patients actually use, and a physiology-centred citation leaves a visible gap there. A single-part award also forgoes any second recognized achievement. I accept these costs because each alternative configuration has a larger credit problem: swapping in Knudsen shifts the prize toward product development, and a second part would require an attribution-complete candidate that I do not see on the shortlist.

responses.point: Linnarsson moved to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov but calls the choice between Mojsov and Knudsen a close call, since his opening ballot made the opposite trade-off, and asks whether a physiology-centred citation can acknowledge the analogues without making Knudsen necessary.
responses.response: I think it can, and that is my answer to the chair's first question. The citation can say that the discoveries of GLP-1 physiology and its active form made incretin-based therapy possible. That credits the upstream discovery on which the analogue chemistry depended and does not claim the chemistry itself. I do not think the acknowledgement requires a name. Your point that the public impact comes from liraglutide and semaglutide is correct, but that is an argument for the importance of the discovery, not for who made the discovery. Your honest statement that this is close is fair, and I would keep it visible in the committee record. If the committee instead wants to reward drug design, that is a different achievement and should be argued as one, with Knudsen as its own named case.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, ranked B024 (imatinib) second and listed it as an alternative, and in round 1 asked whether a second part such as B024 or B006 would strengthen the award or dilute a near-unanimous first choice. He also notes that earlier foundational contributors outside the credited names (Rowley for BCR-ABL, Eshhar for CAR) may limit those alternatives.
responses.response: On the chair's question, I do not see a second part that strengthens the award. The Rowley omission is a real problem for B024: the lesion and its kinase product are the discovery, and the credited names Druker, Sawyers and Lydon represent the drug that exploited it. That makes B024 closer to the product-development case than B017, which I am already defending against that charge. For B006 I share your concern about Eshhar, and I would not give it a seat by default either. I therefore see no defensible two-part configuration inside the three-person limit. A second part would also force B017 below three names. I keep both as alternatives only, in case the committee cannot settle B017, and I do not propose either as a pairing.

responses.point: Perlmann argues that Drucker, Holst and Mojsov are, from the supplied names, the most defensible set that rewards discovery over product development, and that a citation which includes the pharmaceutical step risks rewarding development more than discovery. He also raises whether Knudsen should replace or accompany Mojsov.
responses.response: I agree with the reasoning and with the trio, and I want to take up the question of replacing Mojsov seriously. Replacing her with Knudsen would remove the one name that rests on identification of the active peptide, and it would turn the citation into a hybrid that we would then have to defend on both fronts. Knudsen cannot accompany the three without breaking the three-person limit. Where I differ from you slightly is on how far the priority dispute should weigh. You treat it as a possible claim by uncredited early contributors. I treat it as something the evidence supplied to us cannot decide, so I would not alter the names because of it. I would instead make the citation wording specific to the identification of the active form and not to first detection of any GLP-1 activity, so that it does not assert more than we can verify.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius moved from an opening trio that included Knudsen to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and says that if GLP-1 is settled, a second distinct part (CAR-T or anti-TNF) is worth considering only if its attribution cost is acceptable under the three-person limit.
responses.response: I appreciate that you changed your configuration for a reason that is stated, which is anchoring the citation on the discovery of the hormone's action. On the second part, I would apply your own test of attribution cost. B018 has a clean two-name credit, which is its strength, but the contribution I can see in the supplied evidence is the demonstration that TNF is a therapeutic target. That is a different kind of achievement from B017 and I rank it lower. B006 lacks Eshhar and, as I said in round 1, I would hesitate to narrow it to two names without Rosenberg's role being argued. Given that, I would not add either. I do not dispute that either has large clinical impact. My objection is to the credit structure, not the medicine.

uncertainties: Priority for the active GLP-1 peptide and its insulinotropic role (Mojsov versus Habener and others) cannot be resolved from the supplied evidence, and I have not verified it.
Whether the committee will accept the omission of Knudsen as a stated principle of a physiology-centred citation, or will see it as a gap.
Whether the committee would prefer a second part if B017 is not settled, and whether B006 or B024 can be given attribution-complete configurations within three names.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. I have co-authored eight works with Sten Linnarsson (per my profile, not independently audited) and have co-authored with Jonas Frisén, and I work at Karolinska Institutet. None of these ties involves a credited name on any shortlisted ballot ID or my own work, and I do not request recusal from any ballot. Shared affiliation alone does not establish a conflict. The other members' disclosures in round 1 also involve no shortlisted candidate.
